episodes.title: The Economics Show: China wanted western tech. Now, the tables have turned.
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A deep-dive on China's decades-long strategy of trading market access for Western technology, and whether the US/EU should now mirror that playbook against China. Relevant for an EM trader tracking the structural drivers behind US-China trade tensions, EU investment-screening policy, and China's shift from manufacturing absorber to exporter of advanced tech (EVs, batteries, high-speed rail, wind turbines).

**Key points**
- China's 2018 Section 301 report (basis for Trump-era tariffs) centered on forced tech transfer/IP theft, not trade imbalances — that framing still shapes US-China trade policy today.
- Successes: high-speed rail (50,000km built in 17 years, more capacity than rest of world combined) and wind turbines (China went from 1% to 20-30% of global installed capacity in ~5 years) via local-content requirements and monopsony bargaining.
- Failures/exceptions: semiconductors and Apple avoided forced JV requirements because China was an export-processing hub dependent on foreign multinationals for ~40% of GDP in exports.
- China now uses its own export controls on tech transfer, particularly toward strategic rivals (US, potentially India, parts of Europe), while remaining more open toward Global South countries.
- EU's Industrial Accelerator Act sets conditions on foreign investments above €100mn from countries with 40%+ global production share — aimed squarely at Chinese investment, seeking reciprocal tech spillovers.

**FX / rates implications**
- Underscores the structural, multi-year nature of US/EU-China trade and tech friction — a persistent tail risk for CNY/CNH and broader EM Asia risk sentiment tied to tariff escalation headlines.
- EU's push to formalize investment-screening/tech-transfer conditions (IAA) signals incremental protectionism that could slow Chinese FDI into Europe, a theme relevant to EUR-China capital flow dynamics.
- China's growing willingness to restrict outbound tech transfer to competitors (versus Global South) suggests a widening bifurcation of trade/investment flows — worth monitoring for CNY policy signaling and China's broader capital account stance.

**Watch list**
- Implementation and enforcement of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act investment conditions on Chinese capital.
- Any escalation in China's export-control policy toward Western semiconductor/tech transfers.
- Continued US-China trade negotiations building on the Section 301/tariff framework.

episodes.title: Underlying Inflation Gauges: Trimming Noise or Trimming Signal?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
PIMCO's Tiffany Wilding examines why underlying US inflation gauges (trimmed mean, median measures) are running well below the elevated core PCE print, and argues the recent core PCE acceleration is more noise than signal. This matters for EM FX/rates traders because it shapes the Fed's policy path and, by extension, the dollar and global risk appetite.

**Key points**
- Underlying inflation measures show ~2.2-2.8% y/y through June 2026, versus core PCE at 3.3% (BEA data).
- Core PCE is an outlier versus other measures; core CPI has not shown the same skew drift.
- 2021-2022 episode showed trimmed measures lag turning points when shocks broaden (Dallas Fed trimmed mean stayed near 2% as headline PCE rose above 4%).
- Much of the core CPI/PCE gap is attributed to portfolio management fees and software/AI-related pricing quirks; BEA methodological changes expected to lower reported PCE inflation by 0.2-0.3pp.
- Unit labor cost inflation is currently in line with the Fed's 2% target, supporting the disinflation base case.
- PIMCO's base case: core inflation cools over time and the Fed likely holds its policy rate this year.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed-on-hold base case with contained underlying inflation is broadly supportive of continued carry trades in EM Asia and LATAM high-yielders (INR, IDR, MXN, BRL) as it reduces near-term hawkish repricing risk for the Fed funds path.
- If markets increasingly accept the "noise not signal" framing, UST yields could stay range-bound to lower, capping DXY strength and easing pressure on EM FX funding costs.
- Reduced urgency for the Fed to tighten further is a mild dollar-negative/risk-supportive backdrop for EM carry and duration positioning.

**Watch list**
- Upcoming core PCE and core CPI prints for confirmation of convergence or further divergence.
- BEA's announced methodological revisions to portfolio management and software price indices and their impact on reported PCE.
- Fed communications/FOMC statements referencing underlying inflation gauges (following Chair Kevin Warsh's public emphasis on this debate).

episodes.title: Why US Stocks May ‘Grind Higher’
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs' co-head of global banking and markets argues US equities can keep grinding higher after last week's violent AI-momentum drawdown and V-shaped recovery, with leverage in the AI trade now largely unwound. He pushes back on market pricing for a year-end Fed hike, expects rates on hold, and flags yen intervention and Bank of Japan policy inertia as a lingering risk.

**Key points**
- July was volatile (Iran war re-escalation, Fed-hike fears, tech momentum unwind) but the S&P ended the month unchanged, showing index-level stability versus high single-stock dispersion.
- Speaker expects no Fed hikes this year, contrary to market pricing, citing fading tariff-driven inflation and a likely deal around the Strait of Hormuz.
- AI infrastructure buildout seen as inflationary near-term (resource pressure) but disinflationary once built out.
- Credit spreads have stayed tight despite heavy hyperscaler debt issuance; resilient nominal economy keeps default expectations low, though more new-issue concession is emerging.
- Yen intervention last week aimed at stabilizing Asian markets; speaker argues intervention doesn't work long-term — real stabilization requires the BoJ to normalize rates, unlike the Fed and ECB/BoE which have already normalized post-pandemic inflation.
- House trade: oil (Brent/WTI) settling below $70/barrel later in the year, bullish front-end US Treasury yields given priced-in hikes look attractive, constructive on staying invested in equities.

**FX / rates implications**
- JPY: BoJ policy lag versus Fed/ECB normalization is the core driver of yen weakness; intervention seen as ineffective without BoJ rate normalization — a risk factor for broader Asia FX stability.
- USD/UST: no Fed hikes expected, front-end yields seen attractive/set to rally — a dovish repricing that would be broadly USD-negative and supportive for EM carry if it plays out against current market pricing.
- Oil: expected drop below $70/barrel is disinflationary and favorable for oil-importing EM (India, Philippines, Turkey-type profiles).

**Watch list**
- Upcoming US jobs report and inflation data, flagged explicitly as the key missing pieces for the rate path.
- BoJ policy trajectory and any further yen intervention.
- Credit market new-issue concessions amid heavy hyperscaler AI-related debt supply.

episodes.title: US support for the yen and China's inflation exports
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
US Treasury joined Japanese MOF intervention to buy yen and sell euros last week — the first US-Japan joint FX intervention in roughly 30 years — signalling Washington's backing for PM Takaichi's government. Separately, NatWest highlights a shift in China from exporting deflation to exporting inflation via a "China export price smile," with implications for global disinflation trends.

**Key points**
- Treasury executed intervention (buying yen, selling EUR) after a January rate-check that saw no follow-through; Besent has since discussed the decision publicly.
- NatWest expects BoJ's next hike in October, with some risk of a September pull-forward; the stronger yen from intervention may buy BoJ more patience.
- NatWest expects the Fed to hold in September on softening core inflation and labor data (NFP due Friday).
- USDJPY/rate-differential relationship has broken down over 18 months; JGB fiscal-supply concerns (consumption tax cuts, energy and defense spending) are seen as the bigger yen driver.
- China's export prices jumped from April, driven by both commodity-linked low-end sectors and a policy-driven push into high-end/tech manufacturing; VAT export rebates being rolled back for steel, aluminium, copper, EV batteries (full removal by 2027); CNY up >7% in 2025.

**FX / rates implications**
- USDJPY: intervention caps near-term downside pressure on yen, but durable strength needs BoJ hawkishness or reduced JGB supply concerns — fiscal/monetary tension under Takaichi is the key headwind.
- USD/Fed: a September hold underpins broad EM carry via lower UST yields, supportive for EM Asia and LATAM high-yielders.
- CNY: managed appreciation likely to continue at a moderated pace, a modest global disinflation offset as China exits cheap-manufacturing dominance, raising global goods-price pressure over time.

**Watch list**
- US NFP (Friday) and core CPI trends for Fed September decision.
- BoJ September vs October meeting for hike timing.
- Further JGB supply/demand signals and local investor repatriation flows.
- China export tax rebate rollbacks (EV batteries fully removed by 2027) and CNY fixing trend.

episodes.title: A turning point for US rates?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
HSBC's Macro Brief examines whether US rates are at a turning point, with 10y/30y Treasury yields rising sharply even as the Fed holds policy rates steady, driven by sticky inflation, resilient growth, firmer energy prices, and heavy fiscal supply concerns. This matters for EM traders because higher UST yields and dollar dynamics directly shape EM FX, capital flows, and carry trades globally.

**Key points**
- New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has reduced forward guidance to preserve policy flexibility, raising bond market uncertainty; July FOMC meeting priced only ~35% odds of a hike.
- Core PCE inflation runs at 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% target, with only a marginal 0.1pp dip in June; Fed delivered 100bp of cuts in 2024 and 75bp in 2025, so 2026 hikes would partly reverse those.
- 30-year Treasury yield has pushed past 5.2%, the highest since the 2007-08 GFC, despite the Fed not having raised front-end rates.
- Treasury held coupon (10y/30y) issuance steady for a 10th consecutive quarter in its latest refunding announcement, wary of pushing yields higher with more supply.
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has discussed alternatives to selling Treasuries abroad (citing Japan) to avoid pushing up rates, potentially tapping the Fed balance sheet instead.
- HSBC's base case: Fed stays on hold through 2026-2027 (wait-and-see), but a reacceleration in inflation data could force hikes.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising long-end UST yields and dollar strength from Fed policy uncertainty are a headwind for EM carry trades and could pressure EM Asia and LATAM currencies broadly (INR, IDR, PHP, MXN, BRL) via higher US real rates and tighter global financial conditions.
- Reduced Fed forward guidance implies higher rate volatility around FOMC meetings, which typically raises EM FX hedging costs and could widen EM credit spreads if bond market confidence in Fed credibility wavers.
- Discussion of Japan-related Treasury sale/intervention dynamics is relevant to broader UST demand technicals watched by EM rates desks.

**Watch list**
- Two more US CPI reports and two jobs reports before the September FOMC meeting, bracketing the Jackson Hole symposium (late August).
- Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, which may address AI/productivity's inflation impact and the Fed balance sheet's future structure.
- Next Treasury quarterly refunding announcement for signals on coupon supply changes.

episodes.title: Steven Tananbaum: The Evolution of Credit Investing and AI Opportunities
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs Exchanges interviews Steve Tananbaum, founder/CIO of GoldenTree Asset Management ($70bn AUM), on his credit-investing career, risk process, and current market views including AI's economic and credit-market impact. Mostly a career retrospective with limited direct EM FX/rates content, though it touches broad risk appetite, inflation-linked bonds, and a passing but relevant Argentina sovereign/provincial debt reference.

**Key points**
- AI financing is only ~2% of the below-investment-grade index but is already pressuring that market — spreads out 8-10bps in the past week amid heavy AI-related and private-credit financing.
- Tananbaum's biggest AI concern is economic: if AI-driven growth decelerates, markets will need to mark down growth assumptions; separately he sees opportunity dispersion across IG/HY/private credit depending on where financing needs concentrate (e.g., SpaceX credit spreads reportedly widened 50-60bps).
- Credit spreads are historically tight; in similar past setups (mid-cycle, tight spreads, >2% growth) credit underperforms equities — consistent with 2026 YTD price action through July.
- On emerging markets, cites Argentina as an example: sovereign debt performed strongly the past two years, but GoldenTree found better risk-adjusted returns/recoveries in less-liquid Argentine provincial debt.
- Favors 30-year US TIPS as a top public-market opportunity, seeing real yields near 3% as attractive versus historical sub-2% norms.

**FX / rates implications**
- Tight credit spreads plus elevated AI capex financing needs are a risk-sentiment signal worth monitoring — any AI growth deceleration narrative could trigger a broader risk-off move that typically pressures EM carry trades and widens EM credit/CDS spreads.
- Argentina commentary reinforces continued investor appetite for ARS-linked sovereign/provincial credit, supportive of the ongoing carry trade narrative there.
- Bullish US TIPS view implies a house expectation that real yields stay elevated/range-bound rather than collapsing, a modest USD-supportive undertone for macro positioning.

**Watch list**
- AI-related HY/IG spread widening as a leading indicator of broader credit risk appetite shifting.
- Any further deceleration signals in AI-driven capex/growth data that could prompt global growth downgrades.

episodes.title: How to break China’s chokehold on rare earths
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
The Economist's Economics Show examines the year-long, US/allied push to reduce dependence on China's dominance of rare earth metals and permanent magnets, following China's 2025 export controls that shut auto and electronics factories globally. For a macro trader, this is a supply-chain/strategic-commodities story with implications for industrial policy, capital allocation, and China's use of trade as geopolitical leverage — relevant background for broader China-related trade and tariff risk, though it does not touch FX, rates or central bank policy directly.

**Key points**
- China controls over 90% of global rare earth processing capacity; its 2025 export curbs on seven rare earths forced Ford, Suzuki and others to halt production lines.
- The US launched Project Vault (Feb 2026), a government-backed strategic rare earths stockpile with GM, Lockheed Martin and Alphabet already signed up, though purchases haven't started; the EU lags further behind.
- The US's Mountain Pass mine (MP Materials) supplies 10-15% of global rare earths but only light rare earths; heavy rare earths remain scarce outside China, prompting USA Rare Earth's ~$3bn purchase of Brazil's Serra Verde mine.
- China continues acquiring mines globally (e.g. Chinese-owned rail into Serra Verde), uses export licensing to map rivals' supply chains, and restricts raw materials more than finished magnets to discourage rival industry formation.
- Experts estimate meaningful diversification away from China (to ~50% reliance) will take until 2030-2035; full independence could take decades given mine development lead times (10-15, even up to 29 years).

**FX / rates implications**
- Limited direct FX/rates read-through; this is a structural industrial-policy and trade-security theme rather than a near-term market catalyst, though continued China-US trade friction over strategic materials could resurface as a headline risk for CNY and broader risk sentiment.
- Brazil (Serra Verde), Malaysia (Lynas separation facility) and Namibia rare earth investments highlight incremental foreign direct investment flows worth tracking for BRL and MYR industrial policy narratives, though scale remains small relative to macro flows.

**Watch list**
- Progress/first purchases under US Project Vault (flagged as possible "this year").
- Any renewed Chinese export restrictions on rare earths/magnets as a trade-tension flashpoint.
- EU stockpiling mechanics and funding decisions, still unresolved.

episodes.title: Through the noise: Equities break out
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This Standard Chartered CIO office discussion covers a global equities breakout driven by strong earnings and softer real bond yields, the coordinated US-Japan FX intervention in USDJPY, and heavy US Treasury/corporate bond supply dynamics. While not focused on core EM Asia/LATAM names, the drivers discussed (Fed-linked yields, USD, risk sentiment, carry trades) transmit directly to EM FX and rates.

**Key points**
- Global equities hit new all-time highs on positive earnings and a pause in US real bond yields; ~85% of S&P 500 companies beat consensus vs a 67% long-term average.
- China earnings season begins next week with a positive outlook expected; strategists retain overweight US and Asia-ex-Japan equities, core holdings in Japan/Euro-area.
- AI capex is generating tangible returns (~25-30% ROI for hyperscalers' cloud businesses), but execution risk remains given large, long-dated investment commitments.
- US investment-grade bond issuance hit a record $180bn in June, driven by hyperscaler AI debt; medium/long-end facing indigestion while 1-5yr bonds stay well-bid.
- US Treasury Q3 borrowing estimate raised to $739bn (+$68bn vs May forecast); total issuance projected to rise to $4.9tn by 2028 from $4.4tn in 2026; T-Bills at 23.7% of outstanding debt.
- 2s10s UST curve has steepened materially on front-end terminal-rate repricing and long-end supply pressure.
- Coordinated US-Japan intervention in USDJPY seen as credible in curbing disorderly moves, not reversing trend; BoJ expected to hike once more this year.

**FX / rates implications**
- USDJPY: resistance near 159-160.5, support at 156.3 and 155.23; wide US-Japan rate differential keeps yen-funded carry trades attractive despite higher intervention risk (lower leverage likely).
- Steepening UST 2s10s curve and continued heavy T-bill issuance are relevant reference points for EM local-rates curve positioning and carry calculus.
- Broad risk-on equity breakout and softer US real yields support EM Asia risk appetite and capital flows generally.

**Watch list**
- BoJ next rate hike timing.
- USDJPY levels: 159.0-160.5 resistance, 156.3/155.23 support.
- China corporate earnings season kicking off next week.
- Longer-dated UST auction absorption as issuance climbs toward $4.9tn by 2028.

episodes.title: The Week Ahead - Up and Down
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Nomura's weekly cross-asset roundup covers US CPI/retail sales previews and Fed outlook, BoJ policy dynamics following yen FX intervention, a Norges Bank rate call, and a broad sweep of Asian data (China, India, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia) plus the RBA meeting — all against a backdrop of volatile risk sentiment tied to Iran-related oil headlines and AI-driven equity records.

**Key points**
- Nomura forecasts US core CPI at 0.2% m/m for July, with core PCE (Fed's preferred metric) seen rising to 0.21% m/m in July from 0.13% in June; retail sales expected to soften (-0.2% headline, -0.1% control group).
- Base case: Fed on hold with no rate hikes through end-2027; upside inflation risks flagged from AI-driven semiconductor/memory chip demand and tariff-related supply shocks feeding into core goods.
- Japan: MOF conducted FX intervention (~JPY12tn estimated via BOJ current account data) after USD/JPY hit 164; Japan holds ~$1.3tn in FX reserves, mostly liquid. BOJ base case is an October rate hike, with September flagged as a risk given political pressure to address yen weakness via policy.
- Norges Bank now expected to hold at 4.25% (Nomura reversed its prior hike call) after June inflation surprised to the downside.
- China CPI seen slowing to 0.8% y/y in July (from 1%), PPI steady at -4.1% y/y, credit growth steady at 7.4% y/y; India CPI seen easing to 4.3% y/y; Korea unemployment steady at 2.7%.
- RBA expected to hold at 4.35% unanimously, with updated forecasts likely showing a weaker currency path pushing up medium-term growth/inflation projections.

**FX / rates implications**
- USD/JPY: intervention plus rising odds of a September/October BOJ hike are yen-supportive; hawkish BOJ minutes (due Monday) and Ueda/Himino commentary are near-term catalysts for JPY volatility.
- Broad risk sentiment remains hostage to oil/Strait of Hormuz headlines — Iran deal optimism has driven equity records and lower oil, but renewed Houthi attack reports could reverse this, a key swing factor for EM carry and risk-sensitive Asia FX.
- Soft China CPI/PPI reaffirms weak domestic demand, a mild negative for CNY and regional growth-linked currencies; India CPI moderation supports RBI's easing bias.
- US CPI/retail sales prints next Tuesday are the dominant near-term UST and DXY catalyst given proximity to payrolls.

**Watch list**
- US CPI and retail sales (Tuesday next week); PPI also due.
- BOJ summary of opinions (Monday Aug 10); Deputy Governor Himino speech (Aug 27); Ueda-Takagi political meeting late August.
- Norges Bank policy decision; RBA meeting (Tuesday); China CPI/PPI/credit data; India CPI; Korea unemployment; Singapore/Malaysia Q2 GDP second readings.
- Strait of Hormuz negotiations and Iran-US de-escalation headlines for oil/risk sentiment.

episodes.title: EM Lens: GMO’s Courmes Steers EM Local Bond Bulls
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
GMO portfolio manager Victoria Corm discusses the outlook for EM local currency debt and FX, arguing the asset class remains structurally attractive despite Middle East (Iran-Israel/Iran-US) war-driven oil volatility, citing high EM real yields, proactive EM central banks, improved fiscal buffers, and continued dollar weakness as key supports.

**Key points**
- Markets are pricing ~60% probability of a 25bp Fed hike in September, ~60% for a BoJ hike, and ~80% for an ECB hike, reflecting a hawkish DM central bank bias even as some EM central banks (Indonesia, South Africa) hold dovish and others (Hungary, possibly Brazil) cut.
- EM real yields, especially in Latin America and EM Asia, remain positive and attractive; EM central banks are seen as "ahead of the curve" versus a Fed viewed as behind.
- Bloomberg Dollar Index down roughly 8.1% last year and down again this year; Corm says she is structurally bearish USD and sees EMFX valuations one quartile richer than 2022-23 lows but still with room to run.
- Frontier EM local markets (Nigeria, Egypt, Serbia, Uruguay, Kazakhstan, Dominican Republic, Zambia, Ghana) offer high nominal carry with lower volatility due to managed/pegged FX regimes, resembling pre-2010 South Africa/Turkey/Colombia.
- TWD and KRW models have flipped to overweight for the first time in years on AI-driven terms-of-trade and current account improvement; China excluded from relative-value models as a policy-driven, largely domestic market; traditional havens JPY and CHF no longer behaving as such.

**FX / rates implications**
- Bullish EMFX bias broadly (structural USD weakness, positive EM real rates) supports carry trades across EM Asia and LATAM; Brazil and other high-real-yield names flagged as potential cut candidates if inflation stays contained.
- TWD and KRW upgraded to overweight in RV models on AI-linked terms-of-trade strength — notable positioning shift for North Asia FX.
- Key risk to the bullish EM thesis: a fresh oil/inflation shock from the Iran conflict that compresses EM real rates, or the Fed proving more hawkish/inflation stickier than expected under new leadership.

**Watch list**
- September FOMC meeting (~60% probability of 25bp hike priced) alongside BoJ and ECB hawkish repricing.
- Trajectory of Iran-US/Middle East conflict and oil prices as the swing factor for EM inflation and real-rate buffers.
- Signs of frontier-market overvaluation or balance-of-payment stress as foreign inflows into off-benchmark EM credits increase.

episodes.title: I'm just here for the health benefits
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This Indicator episode opens with a weak US jobs report before pivoting to "job lock" — the phenomenon of workers staying in jobs they dislike solely to keep employer-provided health insurance. The jobs-market weakness and rising job lock both point to a labor market losing dynamism, relevant background for Fed policy watchers even though the episode's focus is domestic health policy rather than markets.

**Key points**
- July payrolls fell by 23,000, worse than economists expected; May and June figures were revised down by a combined ~100,000 jobs.
- Unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, but only because roughly 260,000 people left the labor force (not due to hiring strength).
- A Gallup survey found ~23 million adults (about one in four workers) are in health-benefit-related job lock, up from ~16% five years ago.
- Average family health insurance premium is now ~$27,000/year; ACA subsidy expiration at end-2025 drove a 58% average increase in out-of-pocket premiums for enrollees.
- Healthcare has overtaken gas prices as Americans' top economic worry, per KFF polling.

**FX / rates implications**
- The weaker-than-expected payrolls print and large downward revisions reinforce a cooling-labor-market narrative that supports the case for Fed rate cuts — a dovish signal that is USD-negative and UST-yield-negative at the margin, with typical positive spillover to EM Asia and LATAM carry trades via lower US rates.
- Persistent labor-market friction from job lock (reduced worker mobility) is a structural drag on US productivity and wage dynamics worth monitoring for its slow-moving effect on US growth trends.

**Watch list**
- Healthcare policy and ACA subsidy fights are likely to feature heavily in November US midterm elections, a domestic political catalyst with indirect fiscal-policy implications.
- Future Jobs Friday prints and payroll revisions for continued confirmation of labor-market softening ahead of FOMC decisions.
